⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run.
  • Industry observers note that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants.
  • I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Recent findings suggest that nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he right now co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

Industry observers note that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he notes. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

How's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

According to recent reports, for the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Industry observers note that well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

Recent findings suggest that I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

Sources indicate that in terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

Industry observers note that and so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

Recent findings suggest that so I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

According to recent reports, and it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

But thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

And certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

It's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a substantial focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

Sources indicate that that's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

It has been revealed that well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

It has been revealed that and I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some upcoming young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really key to them.

Recent findings suggest that once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

According to recent reports, I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

Industry observers note that I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

In a recent development, it's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

I already love my Gola Elan sneakers, and now they come in fun animal prints that I can't get enough of. I chose the cheetah, but the cow and the dalmatian picks look just as awesome. If you often wear a "uniform," this is a great way to mix it up just a bit. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that these are on my wish list because dark green satin pants make a plain sweater look like a whole holiday look. They’re pull-on with an elastic waistband, so they’re basically fancy pajamas that are still special enough for the party invitation, and the 3% spandex gives them a little stretch for dinner-table lingering. At $98, they’re a pretty easy way to get a brand-fresh outfit out of the one top she already loves! — Katie Garrity.

I discovered the Varley brand on a casual browse of Evereve, hence my newfound obsession with their half-zips! The Maura is the slightly dressier sister to the Milano half-zip, making it the perfect pairing for high-rise jeans or wide-leg trousers. I have a long torso and the cropped, relaxed fit doesn’t feel too short, which is a huge bonus, and I’m obsessed with the foldover collar. — Julie Sprankles.

I love the distinct look of this bag, along with the really neat way that the straps convert from handles to an adjustable cross-body length. The size is also perfect for carrying everything you need on a light day when you don't want a full-sized tote. For people who want ONE nice purse that can be appropriate for a lot of different situations, this is such a great pick. — Sarah Aswell.

A classic leather crossbody is such a smart finishing touch, and this bag earns bonus points for being an affordable designer option, coming in at under $100. It’s crafted from full-grain Italian leather with gold-plated hardware, so you get that timeless style in a petite size that fits all your essentials. It works for errands, is a great go-to travel purse, and is equally excellent to rock on a night out. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I feel like everyone is selling a lounge set this year, and this one is great because it's affordable and super cozy. For under $70, you get three really quality pieces of clothing: a pair of sweatpants, a camisole, and a calf-length cardigan that basically serves as a whole blanket. You can wear them separately or together, and I love that they're nice and warm without making me hot. The cardigan is my go-to when I get cold while working at home. — Sarah Aswell.

I used to never give my socks a second thought, but lately I’ve dipped my toe (hehe) into treating them as part of my outfit and have been surprised by the little dopamine boost I get from it. These Maria La Rosa metallic socks are made in Italy from pure silk and dipped in the prettiest shimmery foil. You can pair them with loafers or mules to make a statement, or wear them underneath a nice pair of slacks for a peekaboo moment. These would be a fancy addition to any mom’s stocking. — Julie Sprankles.

On days when I cannot muster the energy to put much thought into my clothing, a great pair of glasses is kind of like a cheat code for looking polished. These Gucci frames have a bold, glossy square shape that comes across as fashion-forward without being fussy, so I feel like they’d work with everything from an oversized sweater and leggings to a holiday dress. They’re more of an investment than the cheapies Mom might typically order off Amazon, but they come with built-in peace of mind: Gucci craftsmanship, plus Ottica’s 365-day frame and lens warranty. — Julie Sprankles.

One of the parts of aging I'm dealing with is saying goodbye to my high heels. It's sad, but my weak ankles and foot challenges say it's time. But... I don't want to start wearing old lady shoes when I dress up! Enter shoes like these — these flats are comfortable and safe for my feet, but they also look so special when I wear them. And they look good with jeans but can also tag along to your holiday party, no problem. I KNOW they are cool because my teenager steals them. — Sarah Aswell.

I have my eye on this dress for the holidays, and I feel like it would make a great gift for any mom who needs a go-to occasion dress that is beautiful but effortless. The rich green shade feels so festive, and the lace trim is so romantic. Just dreamy all around! I also appreciate that it’s lined so you don’t have to fuss with a slip... and did I mention it has pockets?! — Julie Sprankles.

#32711. Industry News: 46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4157 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.
  • Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture.
  • In a recent development, since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.).

In a recent development, since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

It has been revealed that basically, it’s a substantial ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

This is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

It has been revealed that these cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

According to recent reports, in the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

The Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of major holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that my 15-year-old and I are both massive Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

It has been revealed that seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that indicates “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

Sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this newly introduced classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

This sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

In a recent development, this is a new brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, for the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

Sources indicate that my 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

For the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

It has been revealed that this brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell.

Cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that these I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles.

My kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, if your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity.

I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles.

My daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that these M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles.

The problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a substantial gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that all my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that for years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a newly introduced driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that for the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that my artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles.

For the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity.

This is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this manufacturer has been really great for us. #32709. I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1005 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.
  • We were on a family trip to Fresh York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square.
  • Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to Fresh York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

Recent findings suggest that when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

By tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

It has been revealed that so, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

Sources indicate that then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

Industry observers note that the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

#32708. Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.
  • It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee.
  • But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, crucial for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

It has been revealed that he also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

In a recent development, what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

Industry observers note that I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most key thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

Recent findings suggest that you say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

In a recent development, I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

It has been revealed that I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

Recent findings suggest that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A major part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

In a recent development, she knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

Industry observers note that my first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

According to recent reports, so you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

It has been revealed that I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

Industry observers note that after all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

Recent findings suggest that so this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

Recent findings suggest that turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your upcoming one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

Industry observers note that I have remarked for about 100 years that I wanted to get into embroidery. Whenever I see something embroidered at an antique mall or thrift store, I am enchanted, but... they are not cheap. Even thrifted! So, why not make my own? Clever Poppy is the perfect way to get an introduction to embroidery if you're a newbie like me. In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

There’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. You can’t skip songs, you can’t scroll... you actually listen to an album in its purest form. This record player makes that ritual easy, and it looks good doing it with its cool retro-inspired case and little viewing window. It plays both LPs and singles, and it’s compact enough to move wherever you want. I can’t wait to hit the local thrift stores and start building my vinyl collection. (Worth noting: This turntable does also have Bluetooth!) — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor of Lifestyle & Entertainment.

It has been revealed that for all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! I throw my book into my bag along with all my other crap and typically end up ruining it with crayon marks or crumbs from my kid's latest half-eaten snack. This protective padded sleeve keeps your current reads safe from crushed pages and bent covers (and mystery stains!). — Katie Garrity.

Coloring girlies, if you're not using Ohuhu markers, we need to talk! This 104-color pack is my go-to when I'm having a cozy coloring night with my daughter. Plus, these markers have a dual-tip marker design — choose the brush tip for sweeping, calligraphic strokes, or the fine tip for details. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that I’ve got nothing against my Notes app. In fact, I use it all the time. But I will always, always be a girlie who loves a really beautiful notebook and the way it makes me want to put down my phone and pick up a pen. This journal has a hard cover that comes in some really saturated, beautiful colors; I have the Mulberry and love it, but this Deep Indigo is next on my list! Little thoughtful details just make the notebook a joy to use: thick pages, a ribbon bookmark, a built-in pen holder, and a handy inner pocket. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that for the person on your list who has approximately 10,000 photos living in their phone and zero prints to show for it, a Mixbook photo book is the most meaningful and genuinely beautiful gift you can give. Mixbook is consistently rated one of the best photo book services for quality and customization, with hundreds of gorgeous themes and layouts that make the final product look intentional and special rather than just a dump of your camera roll. The design tool is incredibly easy to use, the printing quality is stunning, and they run sales constantly, which makes a truly luxurious gift very achievable. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, anyone who has an addiction to making sourdough (or eating it like me) will absolutely love this bread bag from Keeki. It’s a beeswax-lined linen bag that stores your loaf and allows the bread to breathe. The natural antibacterial properties of beeswax will help deter mold! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve long been a fan of Papier, so I was pumped to see the brand venture into board games, starting with this gorgeous Midnight Mosaic Chess Set. #32703. Industry News: What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1129 w)

Industry News: What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • Industry observers note that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.
  • Sources indicate that we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

Industry observers note that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

Sources indicate that we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

“I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” says Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

Inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

Recent findings suggest that “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas says.

Sources indicate that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, claims Melas.

Ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

It has been revealed that “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He mentioned that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas says.

Recent findings suggest that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

It has been revealed that “We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee indicates that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas says she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

In a recent development, “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a significant, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she indicates. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

In a recent development, since 2001, October 16th has been known as National Feral Cat Day â an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and give a voice to the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. It is estimated that there are around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, and we know that it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming. Thatâs why many feline rescue groups want to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month.

Leading the charge is Mission Meow, a unique organization that supports small feline-focused nonprofits with impactful grants, helping to deliver lasting transformations for cats in need. Throughout the year, they coordinate with donors to provide much-needed funding to animal charities across the country, giving smaller groups the means to continue their vital work. To celebrate Mission Meowâs 4th Anniversary and #FeralCatAwarenessMonth, the latest round of grant recipients have been selected in recognition of the work they do to address one of the biggest challenges facing cat rescue: overpopulation.

One of the most impactful initiatives in managing stray and feral cat communities is Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR).

âTNR tackles the problem at its source by humanely reducing the number of kittens being born outdoors while improving the lives of existing community cats,â notes Sally Williams, founder and CEO of Mission Meow. âWith our anniversary falling during Feral Cat Awareness Month, it felt like the perfect opportunity to shine a light on this critical work and invest in organizations creating long-term, sustainable change.â.

With that in mind, five nonprofit organizations were selected for this round of Mission Meow grants:.

Community Cat Welfare Network in Pinehurst, North Carolina supports the humane welfare and stabilization of existing community cat colonies in central North Carolina through the provision of food, insulated winter shelters, veterinary care, humane population stabilization efforts, and public education.

Grant funding will provide 20 winter shelters for stabilized community cat colonies.

Through the work of Fix & Feed Feline Feral in Tampa, Florida, stray cats and kittens are humanely trapped and spayed or neutered, vaccinated for rabies, and returned to their colonies, which are managed by caring volunteers. The health of these feline communities is supported through health checkups, annual vaccinations, and specific health care as needed.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment and an incubator to expand their growing community program.

Lupa Legacy Animal Rescue provides medical care to homeless pets in central Oklahoma, with a focus on owner-surrendered pets and tame, stray cats and kittens from TNR efforts.

Grant funding will help provide TNR equipment and microchip readers to expand trapping efforts to a nearby trailer park.

Hands to Paws Rescue in Georgia initiates and supports programs that extend and elevate the standards of compassionate care for companion animals in the greater Augusta area by providing educational programs, direct care, and cooperative efforts to increase access to low-cost spay/neuter, rescue, fostering, and adoption of animals.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to help expand their community cat spay/neuter transportation program.

Sources indicate that tippedEars in Compton, California, is combating cat overpopulation through humane TNR. While in their care, community cats are sterilized, vaccinated, and treated for fleas.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to create a trap-lending program for trained community members.

Industry observers note that each organization stood out in its own unique way, but they all shared qualities that are deeply notable to Mission Meow. They are collaborative, community-focused, and committed to TNR, addressing cat overpopulation at its source. Many work with underserved communities and focus on community cats who could easily be overlooked. Most importantly, they understand that creating lasting change means not only helping the cats in front of us today, but also working to prevent more cats from needing help tomorrow.

Industry observers note that even little changes can have a huge impact, and there is no such thing as a âsmallâ donation â every little bit helps. Start at home by supporting local animal shelters and TNR programs, spay & neuter your cats, and when youâre looking for a new feline friend, think adoption first.

3 Ways To Stop Your Kid From Being A Walking Petri Dish, Per A Pediatrician

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician indicates these three habits get you pretty close.

Most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

According to recent reports, “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

Recent findings suggest that then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more key for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

Sources indicate that “Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most important times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

In a recent development, “Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

Beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

In a recent development, additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

Industry observers note that “Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” states Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

Industry observers note that since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom indicates to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

In a recent development, taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he said “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

The Silent Health Problem Vets Say Most Cat Owners Never See Coming
