How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.
  • Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged?
  • Industry observers note that all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

Industry observers note that all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

Medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

According to recent reports, “There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” indicates Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”.

Lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh states, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”.

According to recent reports, both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” says McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:.

It has been revealed that an absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh says that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too substantial, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”.

Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

Our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

Industry observers note that while it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something new for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

According to recent reports, mcHugh recommends trying out latest topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” indicates McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”.

Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

Sources indicate that since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes states it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

In a recent development, for using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”.

Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:.

Illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

In a recent development, “[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” says McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”.

When our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

Sources indicate that “When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”.

Authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:.

In a recent development, âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he noted.

The dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal issues, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

Sources indicate that following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Industry observers note that some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

They didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Industry observers note that evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

It has been revealed that french Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a big part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â.

A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

Sources indicate that these concerns have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

That little flat face. Those substantial eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

Most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

Sources indicate that A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

There is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

Recent findings suggest that the more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

This does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

A female dog becomes a breeding machine.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

When it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

Sources indicate that if you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare matter, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

It has been revealed that when extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:.

Are they breathing comfortably?

Do they have functional airways?

And, as the horrific plight of these 48 dogs reminds us, where did they come from?

Loving Bulldogs is not the problem.

The problem is loving an appearance so much that we stop asking what that appearance means for the animal.

These dogs have been through a terrible situation, but now they have a chance.

In a recent development, they need veterinary care. Their nails need treatment, their skin and eyes need evaluation, their nutritional needs need to be addressed, and their other medical problems need to be properly investigated. Some require specialized treatment, while others are recovering in foster homes.

And hopefully, many of these dogs will eventually experience something that should have been completely ordinary from the beginning:.

According to recent reports, these dogs were not born to produce puppies. They were not born to be quiet. They were not born to look a certain way for someone else's profit.

For that reason, adoption should always be considered before buying a puppy.

There are so many wonderful dogs already waiting in shelters, foster homes, and recovering from neglect. Dogs that may not have the perfect face or pedigree but have an enormous capacity to love.

They don't need to be produced.

Please, before asking where to buy the puppy with the cutest face, ask who is already waiting for someone to choose them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The real must-haves, how to prevent diaper rash from day one, and where your budget actually matters.

Bringing a baby home is exhausting, but at least you know how to prepare. Or do you? Every time you turn your phone on, there’s a latest product being advertised that your baby absolutely must have. News flash: they don’t. Babies aren’t influencers. They don’t need a 12-step skincare routine, and you don’t have to buy a wipe warmer to be a good parent.

It has been revealed that pediatric guidance necessitates a much shorter list than your feed does. Here’s what you actually need to focus on.

Having a newborn is chaotic enough (IYKYK); your checklist shouldn’t add to it. File these under real must-haves:.

That’s it, truly. Everything else is a nice-to-have you can just buy later.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll be changing a lot of diapers every day, so one of the most notable things you can do is establish a good diapering routine. This is what you need within arm’s reach:.

It all comes down to what’s in the wipe and how reactive your baby’s skin is. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding fragrances, dyes, and parabens on infant skin, so that's a good place to start.

The bottom line: For most newborns, a fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe is just fine. Don't worry about water wipes unless your baby's skin reacts to everything.

Recent findings suggest that most diaper rash is the byproduct of moisture and friction, so the best way to prevent it is to establish a good changing routine. Here’s what the AAP advises:.

Call your pediatrician if the rash:.

It goes without saying that this checklist doesn’t replace your pediatrician’s advice. For questions or concerns about a lingering diaper rash, call them.

Babies are not cheap! You'll be blowing through roughly 240 to 360 diapers a month. Here are some ways you can save:.

Prioritize fit and leak protection.

According to recent reports, make your diaper budget work for you. Fewer leaks and blowouts mean fewer outfit changes (and fewer middle-of-the-night sheet swaps). So, the convenience alone will pay for itself. You don’t even have to trade up to a premium line to get it: Mainstream Pampers lines like Swaddlers and Baby Dry cover the pediatric-aligned basics. Store-brand diapers offer a lower-cost option for budget-conscious parents.

Industry observers note that if your baby's skin isn't super reactive, there’s no need to splurge on specialty wipes. A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive-skin wipe'll do the trick.

Weigh a subscription vs. buying separately.

Here are five picks, drilled down by category:.

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

According to recent reports, stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding blueprint requires. Everything else can wait.

Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

Fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

Sources indicate that two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

Industry observers note that prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

It has been revealed that this is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

Recent findings suggest that the same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

  • Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Sources indicate that dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

Dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

The key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

According to recent reports, naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

It has been revealed that feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

According to recent reports, training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Industry observers note that digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Industry observers note that gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Industry observers note that avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

Sources indicate that for dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

In a recent development, as we drove through the beautiful mountain scenery surrounding Lake Chapala, I wasnât sure what to expect. Julie Wittmann picked me up early in the morning, and now we were on our way to help distribute food to families who needed extra help feeding their pets.

In a recent development, when we arrived, large sacks of cat and dog food had already been divided into individual portions by a team of Pet Food Bank Lakeside volunteers who gather every week to prepare the food for distribution. We moved the bags into two piles, one for each community they would serve, ready to be collected by volunteers who would take them to families in need.

It was simple work, but it was part of a much greater effort.

Pet Food Bank Lakeside is an independent partner of FoodBank Lakeside, which provides âdespensasâ (bags of basic groceries and household essentials) to families experiencing financial hardship. Families receiving assistance are asked how many pets they have, helping connect the two programs. The pet food program now provides food for more than 1,200 dogs and cats each month.

Next, Julie and I headed to the small town of Santa Cruz, joined by FoodBank Lakeside leader Steve Motenko, his wife Karen, their granddaughter, her best friend, and Javier, a cheerful local with a kind heart. Javier knows the families in the community and helps coordinate the deliveries.

Sources indicate that everyone we met was struggling financially. For most, that hardship was compounded by illness, age, or disability. We met a woman who was completely blind and several people who used wheelchairs.

Just like us, many have pets, and just like our own cats and dogs, theirs are companions, confidants, and cherished members of the family. For some of the people we met, who spend much of their time at home because of age or a health condition, their pet may be their most constant companion.

In a recent development, looking at them, it was impossible to see a dog or cat as simply another expense. These animals were part of the family. They brought comfort, protection, affection, and, very often, a little joy into lives that could use more of it.

That is something Julie and FoodBank Lakeside understand well. Helping someone feed their pet is not just about putting food in a bowl. It is about helping preserve a very important relationship.

According to recent reports, as we moved from house to house, we also carried treats for the dogs we met along the way. They rapidly learned that the cars arriving meant something good was coming.

Sources indicate that one particularly enthusiastic dog decided not to wait for us at home. He followed our cars from one house to the next, keeping pace for two or three stops as if he had appointed himself our unofficial escort.

It was a small, funny moment in an otherwise emotional morning, and it brought plenty of smiles from everyone.

What I noticed most was how happy most of these people were to see the volunteers arrive.

According to recent reports, these were not strangers arriving at a doorstep with a bag of food. There were smiles, conversations, and a sense of familiarity that comes from years of showing up for the same community.

One visit made that especially clear.

Sources indicate that one of the women who had received help from the FoodBank for her cat had passed away only days before we arrived. Karen told me through tears that they had known each other for six years and had become very close. She described her as one of the sweetest women she had known.

The friendship had grown both ways. Over the years, the woman had prepared plant cuttings for Karen and given her handmade embroidery pieces as Christmas gifts. These were small gestures, but they spoke of a relationship that had grown far beyond a food delivery.

Her cat was still there, and the womanâs daughter was relieved to know that the pet food program would continue to help care for it.

Industry observers note that I found that moment difficult to forget. The woman was gone, but the connections she had made remained in Karen's memories, in the plants she had shared, in the handmade gifts she had given, and in the cat still waiting at home.

That is something you cannot measure in bags of food, but in kilos of love instead.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

After moving from Portland, Oregon, to the Lake Chapala area, she began looking for ways to help animals in her fresh community. When COVID-19 disrupted daily life, she asked local veterinarians what they believed was needed most.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

It has been revealed that today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year upgrade, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

But Julie's work goes beyond food.

Julie and her volunteers also visit local schools to teach children about pet care.

For Julie, education is one of the most crucial ways to prevent animals from being misunderstood or mistreated.

âEducating children is particularly important,â Julie explains. âWhen they understand that the weird-looking dog has scabies, and that what it needs is medication, we prevent that dog from being mistreated and left aside.â.

Sources indicate that her point is simple. Children need to understand what they are seeing before they can respond with compassion.

She sees the same principle in the way children learn what animals need.

âThe only way for kids to understand that it is not normal for dogs to spend all day tied up to a post is to let them know that this is not normal, to teach them what dogs are, what they need, and how they can enrich each other's lives.â.

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

In a recent development, during our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and says she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

What struck me was that these deliveries were about so much more than food. They were about people knowing, caring for, and looking out for one another.

Javier knew the families. Karen had formed a six-year friendship with one of the women we visited. Volunteers gathered each week to prepare food. Teenagers came along to help. Julie kept showing up for the pets.

The work had become a community.

Julie notes it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â.

After spending that morning with her, I understood that belief in a more personal way.

When someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very important companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Helping them keep those animals fed also helped them keep an important part of their lives.

By the end of the day, I felt an enormous admiration for Julie and for the people who have joined her in this work.

In a recent development, I had arrived thinking I was just going to help deliver pet food. Instead, I witnessed something much bigger. I saw people who had built genuine relationships with their neighbors. I saw volunteers giving their time week after week. I saw teenagers learning to help others. I saw a daughter relieved that her mother's cat would continue to receive food.

Most of all, I saw how much a small act of kindness can mean when someone is having a difficult time.

My heart felt very warm on the drive home.

I kept thinking about those bags of food we had divided into two piles that morning.

At first, they had simply looked like bags of pet food waiting to be delivered.

By the end of the day, I understood what they represented.

And, sometimes, the chance for a person and the animal they love to stay together.

I've watched it happen more times than I can count â the exact moment a long-stay shelter dog stops being "a shelter dog" and starts just being a dog. It usually happens somewhere in the middle of an adventure.

Recent findings suggest that that moment is what inspired me to start Ariana's Doggos. Because when a dog has spent months living in a kennel, the version of them you see through the bars isn't necessarily their true self.

Dogs have always grounded me. They bring joy, companionship, and a sense of home, often asking for nothing in return. I started Arianaâs Doggos because I believe every shelter dog deserves to be seen for their potential, not just as an animal waiting behind bars. I know that every dog sitting in a kennel could be a companion, adventure buddy, couch potato, comedian, walking partner, and family member. They just haven't met their person yet.

In a recent development, I started Ariana's Doggos because I wanted to give long-stay shelter dogs the opportunity to simply be dogs outside the shelter environment, while capturing those experiences for potential adopters see them too. I don't just want to show people a dog's face and tell them that they're sweet. I want to show them what that dog could actually look like in their life.

Recent findings suggest that what does this dog look like walking through a park? Do they love sniffing trails? Do they want to chase a toy around a pet store? Are they goofy? Are they cuddly? Do they want to say hello to every person they meet?

Those are the moments that can help someone imagine, "I could see this dog living with me.".

It has been revealed that before Ariana's Doggos, I worked in fundraising, media, and storytelling. I spent three years working for a fundraising app, seeing firsthand how vital community support can be. I've always been drawn to production and storytelling, and previously worked as a radio producer. Eventually, I realized that audio alone wasn't filling my creative cup. I wanted to create something deeply visual and emotionally impactful.

At the same time, I became increasingly interested in rescue dogs and saw firsthand how the stress of a long shelter stay can affect them. I knew some rescues already gave dogs opportunities to leave the facility for walks or special outings, but I kept thinking about what could happen if those experiences became continuous storiesâthe difference between someone scrolling past a static photo and stopping to think, "Maybe that's my dog.".

Ariana's Doggos started as a personal media passion project about two years ago, based in Calgary, Alberta. This year, I've begun turning it into a more structured community initiative involving shelters, local businesses, sponsors, and people who simply want to see these dogs get a little more attention.

Something key to understand about shelter dogs is that a kennel is an extremely specific, highly stressful environment. A dog may be overwhelmed, overstimulated, shut down, or frustrated by everything happening around them. Rightfully so â they don't understand why they're there.

Shelter staff and volunteers who care for these animals daily see glimpses of their true nature, but an adopter on the other side of the kennel door rarely sees beyond the first impression.

In a recent development, A dog sitting quietly in a corner or barking like mad can be easy to overlook. That same dog walking beside you through a park, stopping to sniff a tree, looking up at you with a goofy expression, or happily carrying around a latest toy tells an entirely different story.

And sometimes that story is what gets them noticed.

As rewarding as the outings are, there is also a side of this work that breaks my heart.

Industry observers note that the first time you take a dog out, they can be absolutely ecstatic. Everything is new. They're sniffing, exploring, and soaking everything in.

It has been revealed that but when a dog has been waiting for a home for a long time, that excitement can start to change. They seem to understand the routine now. We're going somewhere, we're going to have fun, and eventually, we're going back to the kennel.

That's also why I believe so strongly in the importance of foster homes and other individualized resources for long-stay dogs. Foster homes are an amazing temporary solution for many dogs, but foster networks are always limited, and more dogs will always be waiting for the right foster environment or a spot to open up.

Sources indicate that not every dog has an immediate foster match; some need a very specific environment, routine, or space. When those resources aren't available, dogs can remain in shelters for months. And the longer they wait, the easier it can be for people to overlook them. That's exactly why I keep showing up with a camera and a leash â every video is one more chance for the right person to finally notice them.

It has been revealed that right now, my focus is simple: one dog at a time. Taking shelter dogs out, creating meaningful experiences and exposure for them, and turning those adventures into story-driven videos that reach people far beyond the shelter walls.

Recent findings suggest that with Ariana's Doggos, the outing doesn't end when the dog goes back. The digital story keeps working long after the day is over, putting dogs in front of potential adopters.

I also have a bigger, long-term dream. Eventually, I would love to build a dedicated, foster-scale facility that could work alongside existing shelters and foster networks.

Recent findings suggest that it wouldn't replace shelters or traditional foster homes. Instead, I envision it as a centralized resource for shelter dogs who need extra exposure to find a home, basic training to help them fit into the right home, or a more individualized setting for dogs struggling with the shelter environment.

Most importantly, I want that environment to combine professional care with maximum public visibility through media and storytelling, preparing them fully for their future families.

I don't know exactly what Ariana's Doggos will look like years from now. Right now, I'm still building the foundation through these individual adventures and learning what works.

Every time I take a dog out, I'm reminded that these animals are so much more than their shelter profile.

It has been revealed that they're goofy,  complicated, affectionate. They're curious and occasionally chaotic. They're individuals. They can become such an crucial part of someone's life, and they deserve to be seen that way.

According to recent reports, I may not be able to find a home for every shelter dog, but I can give them a day where they aren't a shelter dog. They're just a dog.

Recent findings suggest that sniffing a trail, choosing a toy, meeting a stranger, or getting the zoomies. A dog discovering something new.

And I can take those moments and put them in front of potential adopters who may never have looked twice at them in a kennel.

Because sometimes finding a dog a home starts with being seen.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.
  • According to recent reports, my Nana was not a good cook.
  • Her baking though, now that was good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

According to recent reports, my Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

Her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

It has been revealed that most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great big smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

Sources indicate that she made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a latest love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

In a recent development, her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

Industry observers note that it has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

According to recent reports, it is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a major pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

Industry observers note that it was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

The food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

Industry observers note that jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

How to thank school support staff this American Education Week (Hint: It’s not a mug)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse.
  • That nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did.
  • People like her have a name in education circles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse. She was warm and welcoming, always quick with a comforting hug. More importantly, she had the best Band-Aids in the building, and she wasn’t stingy about giving them out. A scraped knee got one. So did a paper cut, and even some invisible injuries, too. She knew when a kid headed to see her, it wasn’t necessarily about needing that Band-Aid.

That nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did. There were kids who came to her office with a belly ache that wasn’t a stomach bug, but because they hadn’t had breakfast, and possibly dinner either. There were kids who could barely stay awake in class because they’d spent the night in a car instead of a bed. She met those kids with the same warmth she gave my Band-Aid collector, and I’m certain she kept a stash of snacks in her desk for those visits in particular.

People like her have a name in education circles. They’re education support professionals, or ESPs, and they include school nurses, cafeteria workers, bus drivers, security staff, paraeducators, technical personnel, custodians, skilled trade workers, and front office staff. Ask kids about their favorite grown-up at school, and there’s a decent chance the answer is one of them.

The people our kids adore are often the people schools pay the least. Nearly 32% of full-time ESPs earn less than $25,000 a year, according to the National Education Association, and on average, they’re paid below a living wage in all 50 states.

That’s not a livable wage in most areas. “Our wages are so low, we are forced to have two or three jobs,” paraeducator Yahaira Rodriguez told NEA Today. The nurse who stays late with a hungry kid may be heading to a second job after school, eating dinner in the car on the way. That’s a long day for someone whose job is to take care of everyone else’s kids. It also makes it hard to stay in the job. Before the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported trouble filling at least one non-teaching position, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That means the kids who rely on them the most are the ones who lose out when they leave or the positions can’t be filled.

According to recent reports, the NEA ESP Bill of Rights lays out what these professionals need to stay in the jobs our kids depend on. Developed by ESPs themselves, it asks for pay that covers the bills without a second job, health care they can afford and a workplace ‘free of violence, including physical, verbal, and emotional abuse.’ It’s a practical document about what it takes to keep these jobs filled. The full list includes:.

Since the movement began, 18 states have debuted ESP Bill of Rights campaigns, according to NEA.

American Education Week runs November 16 to 20, 2026, and this year NEA is using it to honor education support staff. Here are a few ways to show up for the people who show up for our kids:.

According to recent reports, our kids won’t remember most of what happened at school, but they’ll remember who was kind to them there. For a lot of them, that’s a nurse, a cafeteria staff or a bus driver doing the job on less than a living wage. Sign the ESP Bill of Rights pledge and help them stay.

According to recent reports, chewing is simply part of being a dog. Whether itâs a young puppy trying out those pointy, latest teeth on the corner of the couch, a teenage pooch chewing on shoes to relieve boredom, or an older dog deciding their toys just arenât cutting it anymore, dogs of all shapes and sizes like to chew.

Most appropriate chew options fall into one of two categories, each with its own distinctive downsides.

Recent findings suggest that the first category is chews that dogs love to chew! The mouth-watering, often very stinky, great-tasting chews like bully sticks, dried tendons, and smoked bones. According to recent reports, apparently, part of adulting is developing a genuine appreciation for cooking. Who would’ve thought?

Now, I’m not saying I’m in my Julia Child era by any means. But I do dabble with scratch-made pasta sauce and homemade spicy beef noodles. That said, when it comes to lazy nights at home or feeding a crowd, I’m never opposed to taking a few shortcuts... especially when they save me both time and money.

As someone who exclusively grocery shops at Trader Joe’s, I’ve tried just about every side dish in the book. Whether you’re finalizing your Taco Tuesday menu or looking for a few last-minute additions to your holiday feast, TJ’s has plenty of options to please everyone at the table, even the picky little eaters. Better yet, some of these can pull double duty at both breakfast and dinner.

Sources indicate that and to sweeten the deal, all these side dishes from Trader Joe’s make multiple servings for less than $6. Now that’s something worth adding to your cart.

It has been revealed that breakfast called, it wants an upgrade. This roasted potato, pepper, and onion medley brings a little room-service flair to your morning, with barely more effort than a few tosses in the pan. Serve it alongside steak and eggs, ideally over easy or poached — but it’s your breaky, your rules.

It has been revealed that (Tip: It also makes a pretty delicious dinner side with bratwurst or pork chops. Turns out, it’s got range.).

Looking for a dinner party side that would even wow the socks off Ina Garten? These kung pao Brussels sprouts are just the ticket. Tossed in a sweet-meets-spicy sauce of hoisin, soy, brown sugar, ginger, garlic, and chili peppers, they're packed with flavor and ready to hit the table in just three minutes. Yes, three. Thank you, microwave!

Recent findings suggest that newly introduced to the TJ’s freezer aisle is this cook-and-serve creamy corn concoction. Sweet corn gets the royal treatment in a rich, velvety sauce made with milk, cream, butter, cheddar cheese, and shallots. Not too shabby for just $4.

Recent findings suggest that when chips won’t do, grab a fork and TJ’s Mediterranean orzo pasta salad to pair with your sandwich. The mini pasta salad features orzo, crumbled feta cheese, chopped red onion, purple olives, and sun-dried tomatoes.

These vanilla bean whipped sweet potatoes aren’t your mother’s sweet potatoes. Sure, they’ve got the usual suspects (nutmeg and brown sugar), but the real star of the show is vanilla bean paste and tiny flecks of vanilla bean seeds. Bet you didn’t see that twist coming, did ya? Go ahead and add this one to your holiday menu.

According to recent reports, is it Taco Tuesday already? Round out your spread with homemade margaritas and TJ’s microwavable Spanish rice. Growing up in a Mexican household, I was spoiled with my mom’s cooking. But I have to admit, this store-bought version has gone platinum in my apartment.

Industry observers note that add some greenery to your chicken and rice bowl with these garlicky shiitake green beans. You can even toss in some mushrooms or diced carrots for extra nutrients and color.

In a recent development, one of my favorite TJ’s dinners is flank steak with a side of mushrooms and Joe's mac 'n cheese. As much as I love scratch mac and cheese, sometimes convenience wins. I’m more than willing to pop this frozen bad boy in the microwave and call it a day.

In a recent development, personally, I’d rather prepare my meat entrées in-house than fuss over the sides. That’s where this freezer-section find comes in handy. This vegetable fried rice is loaded with carrots, edamame, corn, green peas, leeks, and red bell peppers, all tossed in a savory blend of soy sauce, rice wine, onion, sugar, seaweed, salt, and sesame oil.

It has been revealed that it’s never a bad idea to have a few bags of frozen sweet potato fries on hand. And when it comes to dipping sauces, Trader Joe’s has plenty of options to keep things interesting.

Risotto is one of those dishes I’d rather leave to the experts. Luckily, the grocer has a convenient shortcut that goes from freezer to table in just five minutes. Trade rice for this creamy risotto the next time you make salmon or roasted chicken.

Pair this tomato feta soup with a sandwich, salad, quesadilla, or grilled cheese for an easy pick-two lunch combo. It’s also easy to pack for the office!

Inspired by Mexican cuisine, this classic side is best paired with skirt steak, chicken fajitas, enchilada casserole, or homemade burritos. For a quick upgrade, mix it with mayo, cotija cheese, and chili powder to make elote.

Imagine enjoying mashed potatoes without any of the heavy lifting. (I will be blaming my inevitable carpal tunnel on my potato peeler.) Give these a little homemade flair by dressing them up with butter and fresh herbs.

We’ll leave you with a healthy option: TJ’s riced cauliflower stir-fry. Your salmon filet won’t look lonely next to this medley of green peas, cauliflower rice, red bell peppers, grilled corn, and spring onions.

Drinks You Can Make By The Batch

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that bring something good.
  • In a recent development, holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater.
  • According to recent reports, these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

In a recent development, holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

According to recent reports, these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

Industry observers note that julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she mentioned.

A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

Bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

Bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

In a recent development, everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner noted. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

Get the recipe at Cocktails Distilled.

In a recent development, champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done. If the finished punch tastes a little dull, Chamberlain recommends adding a few dashes of Angostura or cardamom bitters to give it more personality.

Industry observers note that love your friends. Not enough to muddle each of them a mojito. Averie Sunshine’s pomegranate mojito punch at Averie Cooks combines white rum, mint, pomegranate juice and seeds, lemon and sparkling water in one pitcher. It makes four generous drinks, so double it for a bigger gathering. Chill the liquids ahead, then muddle the mint and assemble the punch just before serving so the leaves stay fresh, and the bubbles don't disappear. Ice goes in the glasses. One round of muddling. Everybody gets a drink.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

Here, Chamberlain pairs pear nectar with gin, ginger liqueur, rosemary syrup, lemon, cardamom bitters and dry bubbly in her Calling Card Punch. It's an elegant, herbal alternative to the usual holiday punch and serves six to eight. Make the rosemary syrup ahead, chill the ingredients and add the sparkling wine while serving.

It has been revealed that “I tend to build my punch a little less sweet and then I’ll often have a little extra syrup I can add if it seems unbalanced,” Chamberlain mentioned. It's easier to add sweetness than take it away.

Recent findings suggest that by the time dessert rolls around, the adults deserve something stronger than another cup of coffee. McIntosh combines vodka, espresso or cold brew, coffee liqueur and peppermint syrup for a holiday spin on the espresso martini. Her large-batch version makes about 16 servings, with no individual shaking required. Mix everything ahead, chill it in the freezer for about two hours and give it a quick whirl in the blender if you want that signature foam. Pour into a punch bowl and let everyone help themselves. Crushed candy cane rims are optional. You've already done enough decorating.

It has been revealed that give the alcohol-free drinks their own spot at the party. America’s Test Kitchen combines cranberries, ginger, rosemary, cinnamon and star anise in a sweetened base you can make up to four days ahead. When guests arrive, add chilled cranberry juice, orange juice and seltzer. It makes 16 servings, enough for an open house where another family keeps appearing in the doorway.

Get the recipe at America’s Test Kitchen.

The tiny apple leaves are optional – you have enough crafts coming home from school. Chamberlain’s Fallen Leaves Punch mixes cognac, tart apple cider and lemon with homemade cranberry-cinnamon syrup for eight servings. It's a good Friendsgiving option if you want something tart, fruity and a little stronger than cider.

Recent findings suggest that “In terms of flavor combinations, it’s hard to disappoint with the combination of seasonal spice and fruit,” Chamberlain mentioned. Make the syrup ahead, squeeze the lemons the day of and stir everything over a large ice block at serving.

In a recent development, taco night doesn’t need a November makeover. McIntosh makes six spicy margaritas right in the tequila bottle, giving you a batch and a carrying container in one. You'll need to pour out some tequila first; the recipe tells you how much. Mix everything in the bottle, then let it sit in the freezer for 2 to 4 hours, then pour it over ice into salt-rimmed glasses. All the fun of margaritas without anyone spending the evening squeezing limes.

Sources indicate that apple cider is doing a lot of heavy lifting this holiday season, let it have some rum. Chamberlain's Cider Rum Punch combines tart cider, aged pineapple rum, lemon, orange bitters and a homemade mulling-spice syrup for six servings. She makes it every year, and it's easy to see why. The warm spices play nicely with the fruit without turning the whole thing into a scented candle. Make the syrup ahead, then combine everything in a pitcher with plenty of ice and stir until chilled. Bonus: There's no sparkling wine to worry about going flat.

The kids’ table and Grandma can drink from the same pitcher. McIntosh’s pineapple passion fruit agua fresca blends tropical fruit, lime and agave into six refreshing alcohol-free servings. Frozen passion fruit pulp works, and there are no bubbles to go flat on the drive. Make it up to two days ahead, refrigerate and give it a good stir before pouring over ice.

Sources indicate that after the holiday lights walk, everyone comes home freezing and suddenly needs something warm RIGHT NOW. Sunshine's peppermint white hot chocolate at Averie Cooks combines milk, melted white chocolate and a little peppermint extract. The recipe makes five mugs, but you can easily double or triple it for a houseful of cold kids and grown-ups. Heat everything together over low heat, stirring until the chocolate melts. Don't let it boil, and go easy on the peppermint. A little goes a long way. Add marshmallows if you've got them. Nobody's going to complain.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

Recent findings suggest that the wine people and the margarita people can share a pitcher. Migliarini’s tequila sangria at Beautiful Booze combines Sauvignon Blanc with tequila, cranberry syrup, fresh cranberries, red and green apples and lime. “Keeping it simple, my recipe includes fruits that are available throughout the entire year,” she writes in the recipe. It serves five to six, making it a good choice for a casual Friendsgiving. Chill the wine, tequila and fruit mixture ahead, then add the lemon-lime soda just before serving.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

No fish. Promise. Amy Traynor’s Fish House Punch at Moody Mixologist combines cognac and aged rum with peach liqueur, lemon and cold black tea. Think peach iced tea with considerably more going on. Her recipe includes a version for 10, so there's no need to multiply or do any guesswork. Freeze a large ice block ahead, stir the ingredients over it at serving and finish each glass with freshly grated nutmeg. Fair warning: This one's boozy.

Get the recipe at Moody Mixologist.

It has been revealed that dinner’s over, the kids have claimed the television and nobody’s ready to leave. Put a pot of McIntosh’s mulled Aperol on the stove for the spritz drinkers still on your sofa. Dry white wine, Aperol, apple cider and honey warm with orange and whole spices. It makes six servings and needs just 15 to 20 minutes over low heat. Don't let it boil. Ladle into mugs and let everyone settle in. The kitchen will smell like you had a plan.

Industry observers note that cats = happiness. Itâs an equation that neither cat lovers nor the cats themselves will find surprising, but itâs not something you expect to be evaluated, let alone proven, through scientific research. In a recent correlational study of subjective well-being across 93 countries, researchers examined the relationship between cat density, exposure to Toxoplasma gondii, socioeconomic status, and national happiness, with interesting results.

Sources indicate that according to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context. The key word in this study is correlational. Researchers have not discovered that happiness levels are the result of larger feline populations â ie, a causal relationship â only that there is a notable connection between countries reporting higher numbers of pet cats and those ranked highest on the World Population Reviewâs 2025 report on the Happiest Countries in the World.

So before you trade your antidepressant prescription for a kitten, there are a few things worth understanding.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

Interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

The study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

Sources indicate that we know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. They somehow have the ability to draw a smile on our face without saying a single word, simply by lying on our lap or sitting beside us after a difficult day. Emotional support comes in many forms, and cats seem to know just the right way to make us feel happier, calmer, and more at ease.

It has been revealed that but personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

Hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

In other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

Financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are crucial too.

This wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

It has been revealed that countries with more people showing signs of a recent infection tended to have lower happiness scores. To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Neither provides a perfect timeline of when the infection occurred.

According to recent reports, thereâs another crucial detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Differences in hygiene, food safety, healthcare access, and economic circumstances could influence both infection rates and well-being. After all, health and happiness are difficult to separate from the conditions we live in. Ask anyone who cannot turn on a tap and count on clean, safe water. A parasite may be part of the picture, but so are the everyday resources that help us stay healthy, feel secure, and simply have an easier and more comfortable day-to-day.

It has been revealed that T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

Pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

According to recent reports, cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. A cat who retreats, flattens their ears, or flicks their tail may be asking for space. Ignoring those signs because a human wants affection isn't bonding; it's treating a living, breathing creature like a plush toy.

It has been revealed that good care means respecting those boundaries. Hiding places, elevated resting spots, predictable routines, interactive play, and regular veterinary care all help support feline well-being. Changes in behavior often signal pain or illness, so they deserve attention rather than an automatic label of âbad behavior.â.

And no, not every cat wants to be carried around like a furry handbag. Some barely tolerate being looked at when they're minding their own business. That's not a character flaw. It's a cat making its position very clear.

In a recent development, the study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

For cat families, the practical health advice is simple: litter box hygiene is paramount. Scoop the poop daily, since T. gondii oocysts generally need one to five days after being shed to become infectious. Wash your hands after handling litter, wear gloves while gardening, cook meat thoroughly, and make sure you wash and disinfect fruits and veggies before eating.

Pregnant women and those with a weak immune system should consult their doctor about appropriate precautions. During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

According to recent reports, ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

Sources indicate that A familiar purr, a gentle head bump, or a cat choosing your lap to nap in can brighten an ordinary afternoon and put a smile on anyoneâs face. The 3 a.m. bedroom sprints and hairballs left over the Persian rug, however, remain entirely separate research questions!
